p.src: Now the monster, having bound up Sha Monk, neither came to kill him nor struck him, nor did he utter a single curse against him. He snatched up his steel saber and thought to himself, “The Tang monk is a man of the exalted realm and must understand propriety and righteousness. Surely, after I spared his life, he would not have his disciples come to seize me? Ah! Most likely my wife sent some letter to her country and let the secret slip. I shall go and question her.” The monster’s murderous nature suddenly flared, and he went to kill the princess.

p.src: The princess knew nothing of this. Having just finished dressing and arranging her hair, she came walking over. She saw the monster glaring furiously, his brows knitted and his teeth clenched. Still smiling, the princess greeted him: “Husband, what has upset you so?” With a bark, the monster cursed her: “You faithless, wretched woman! You have no sense of human duty at all. When I first brought you here, you had not a word of complaint. You wear brocade and adorn yourself with gold; whatever you lack, I go and find for you. In every season you have enjoyed comfort, and each day I have loved you deeply. Why do you think only of your parents, without the least devotion to your husband?” At these words the princess was so frightened that she fell to her knees and said, “Husband, why do you speak today as though we must part?” The monster said, “Whether it is I who speak of parting or you who seek it, I do not know. I captured that Tang monk and meant to enjoy him, yet how could you release him without first telling me? It turns out that you secretly wrote a letter and told him to carry and deliver it for you; otherwise, why would these two monks have come attacking my gate and demanded that I send you back? Was this not your doing?” The princess said, “Husband, you have wronged me terribly. When have I ever sent any letter?” The old monster said, “Still you argue! I have caught one of our enemies right here. Is that not proof?” The princess asked, “Who is it?” The old demon replied, “Sha Monk, the Tang monk’s second disciple.” When people face death, none willingly admit their guilt; the princess could only brazen it out with him. The princess said, “Husband, calm your anger for now. Let me go with you and question him. If there truly was a letter, then even if you beat me to death, I shall accept it willingly; but if there was none, would you not be killing your poor wife unjustly?”

p.src: Hearing this, the monster allowed no further argument. He swung out an indigo-blue hand as large as a winnowing basket, seized the noble princess by her luxuriant hair, dragged her forward, and dashed her to the ground. Gripping his steel saber, he came to interrogate Sha Monk and barked, “Sha Monk, how dare the two of you attack our gate without leave? Did this woman send a letter to her country, and did the king order you to come?” Sha Monk lay bound there. Seeing how ferocious the demon was—how he had flung the princess to the ground and now held his saber ready to kill her—he thought to himself, “Clearly she did send a letter, and by doing so saved my master. That is an immeasurable kindness. If I reveal it in a single word, he will kill the princess. Would that not be repaying kindness with enmity? Enough, enough! All the time old Sha has followed my master, I have rendered him not the smallest service. Since I am bound here today, I shall give up this life to repay my debt to Master.” He therefore shouted, “Monster, do not behave so outrageously! What letter could she have sent? Why do you falsely accuse her and seek to take her life? There is a reason we came here to demand the princess from you. It is only because you captured my master and held him in your cave, where he happened to observe the princess’s appearance and circumstances. When we reached the Kingdom of Precious Image to exchange our travel rescript, the emperor showed us a portrait of the princess, whom he had long sought. He asked my master whether he had seen her likeness anywhere along the road, and my master then told him about the princess. He then knew she was his own daughter, bestowed imperial wine upon us, and ordered us to capture you and restore his princess to the palace. That is the truth of the matter. There was never any letter. If you must kill someone, then kill old Sha. You must not unjustly harm an innocent person and so grievously offend against Heaven’s law.”

p.src: When the demon heard Sha Monk speak with such heroic conviction, he dropped his saber, lifted the princess in both arms, and said, “I was rash and boorish for a moment and have greatly offended you. Forgive me, forgive me.” He gathered up her black hair and restored her jeweled coiffure, then gently and tenderly, with a pleasant face and cheerful manner, coaxed her back inside and invited her to the place of honor while he apologized. The princess, being a woman whose feelings readily turned, saw him humbly acknowledge his fault and changed her mind. She said, “Husband, if you cherish the love between us, have Sha Monk’s ropes loosened a little.” At this, the old demon immediately ordered his underlings to untie Sha Monk’s ropes and put him in shackles there. Freed from his bonds and placed in shackles, Sha Monk stood up and thought with secret delight, “The ancients said, ‘Make things easy for others, and things will be easy for you.’ If I had not helped her out, how would she have been willing to ask that my bonds be loosened?”

p.src: The old demon then ordered a banquet prepared so that he might apologize to the princess and calm her fright. When they were half-drunk, the old demon suddenly changed into a bright new robe, took a precious saber and fastened it at his waist. Then he turned, stroked the princess, and said, “Wife, stay home and drink, watch over our two children, and do not let Sha Monk go. While the Tang monk is in that country, I too shall go early and acknowledge my kin.” The princess asked, “What kin will you acknowledge?” The old demon said, “Your royal father. I am his son-in-law, and he is my father-in-law. Why should I not go and acknowledge him?” The princess said, “You must not go.” The old demon asked, “Why can I not go?” The princess said, “My royal father did not win his realm by force of arms and battle; his state was inherited from his ancestors. He was a crown prince from childhood and succeeded to the throne; he has never even ventured far beyond the city gates and has never seen a fierce brute such as you. Your face and form are so hideous that, if he saw you, I fear you would frighten him, and that would end badly. It would be better not to go and acknowledge him.” The old demon said, “If that is so, I need only transform myself into a handsome fellow before I go.” The princess said, “Try transforming yourself and let me see.”

p.src: See how he mounted a cloud and soon arrived in the Kingdom of Precious Image. He brought down his cloud and walked to the outer court gate, where he said to the chamberlain, “The Third Prince Consort has come especially to seek an audience. Please convey the message for me.” The palace herald went before the white-jade steps and reported, “Your Majesty, the Third Prince Consort has come to seek an audience and is now waiting outside the court gate for your summons.” The king was conversing with the Tang monk when he suddenly heard mention of a Third Prince Consort. He asked his officials, “I have only two princes consort. How can there be a third?” The officials said, “This Third Prince Consort must surely be a monster.” The king said, “Would it be well to summon him inside?” The elder was alarmed and said, “Your Majesty, a fiend would not be a fiend if it lacked supernatural powers. He can know the past and future, and he can ride clouds and mist. Whether you summon him or not, he will come in. You may as well summon him and save some loss of face.”

p.src: The king approved the proposal and ordered him summoned, so the monster was brought before the golden steps. He too performed the customary dance and cried long life as he made obeisance. Seeing how handsome and elegant he was, the officials did not dare take him for a monster. They were all mere mortals with fleshly eyes and mistook him for a good man. The king saw his lofty and imposing bearing and took him for a pillar capable of saving the realm. He asked, “Prince Consort, where is your home? From what region do you come? When were you joined in marriage to my princess? Why have you come to acknowledge your kin only today?” The old monster kowtowed and said, “My lord, your servant lives in the Moon-Wave Cave on Bowl-Mountain, east of the city.” The king said, “How far is your mountain from here?” The old monster said, “Not far—only three hundred li.” The king said, “With three hundred li between us, how did my princess reach that place and marry you?” With specious words and feigned sincerity, the monster replied, “My lord, from childhood your humble servant delighted in archery and horsemanship and made his living by hunting. Thirteen years ago, I was out with dozens of household servants, flying hawks and coursing hounds, when I suddenly saw a magnificent fierce tiger carrying a woman on its back and making its way down the mountainside. Your humble servant drew his bow and felled the tiger with one arrow. I took the woman back to my estate, revived her with warm water and broth, and saved her life. When I asked where she came from, she never once mentioned the word ‘princess.’ Had she said at once that she was Your Majesty’s third princess, how could I have betrayed my conscience and married her without permission? I should have brought her into the golden hall and sought some official post, great or small, to bring me honor. Only because she said she was the daughter of common folk did your humble servant keep her at his estate. She was beautiful and I had some talent; our affection was mutual, and thus we married and have lived together all these years. After we married, I meant to slaughter that tiger and invite all our relatives to a feast, but Her Highness told me not to kill it yet. p.src: Because of what she said, your servant untied the tiger and spared its life. Still wounded by the arrow, the tiger fled with flying hooves and tucked tail. Little did I know that, having escaped with its life, it would cultivate itself in the mountains for all these years, refine its body into a spirit, and devote itself to deceiving and harming people. Your servant has heard that in former years several pilgrims came seeking scriptures, all claiming to be the Tang monk from the Great Tang. I believe this tiger killed the Tang monk, took his travel document, and assumed the pilgrim’s appearance so that it might deceive my lord here at court. My lord, the creature seated upon that embroidered stool is none other than the fierce tiger that carried off the princess thirteen years ago. He is no true pilgrim seeking scriptures.”

p.src: At the sight, the king’s soul scattered and his spirit fled. All the officials were so frightened that they fled for cover. A few bold military officers led the generals and commandants in a massed charge, hacking wildly with every kind of weapon. This time, had the Tang monk not been fated to survive, even twenty monks would have been pounded into mincemeat. Fortunately, the divine guardians—the Ding and Jia spirits, the Jiedi, the Merit Officers, and the protectors of the faith—were secretly shielding him from midair, so none of those weapons could wound him. The ministers clamored until nightfall before they finally captured the tiger alive, bound it with iron chains, put it in an iron cage, and confined it in a court chamber.

That evening the ministers dispersed from court, and the demon entered the Silver Peace Hall. Eighteen palace maids and ladies in colorful dress were also chosen to play music, sing, and dance while urging the demon to drink and be merry. The monster sat alone in the seat of honor, flanked on either side by women of enchanting beauty and delicate grace. See how he enjoyed his wine until the second watch, when drunkenness overcame him and he could no longer restrain his savagery. p.src: Now the monster sat inside, pouring and drinking his own wine. After each cup, he dragged the woman over and gnawed a couple of bloody mouthfuls from her. While he feasted within, everyone outside spread the news: “The Tang monk is a tiger spirit.” The wild rumor and clamor spread all the way to the Golden Pavilion posthouse. At that time no one was in the posthouse; only the white horse stood at the manger, eating grass and fodder. He was originally the young dragon prince of the Western Sea. For violating the laws of Heaven, his horns had been sawn off and his scales stripped away; transformed into a white horse, he carried the Tang monk westward to seek the scriptures. When he suddenly heard people saying that the Tang monk was a tiger spirit, he thought to himself, “My master is plainly a good man. A monster must have changed him into a tiger spirit and brought him to harm. What am I to do? What am I to do? Elder Brother has been gone a long time, while Bajie and Sha Monk have sent no word.” He endured only until the second watch, then leaped up and said, “If I do not save the Tang monk now, all our merit and achievement are finished—finished!” Unable to restrain himself, he snapped the reins, shook off saddle and bridle, sprang up, and hastily transformed, becoming a dragon once more. Riding a black cloud, he soared straight into the ninth heaven and looked about. There is a poem as testimony, which says:

p.src: From midair, the Little Dragon King saw the Silver Peace Hall ablaze with lamplight and candles. It turned out that eight candles were burning atop eight great red candelabra. He lowered his cloud and looked carefully: there was the demon, sitting alone above and brazenly drinking wine and eating human flesh. The Little Dragon laughed. “This wretch is no great shakes. He has betrayed himself and exposed his trail; now I know which way the wind blows, he is as good as a weight dropped into a broken basket. Is eating people supposed to be some worthy accomplishment? I still do not know what has become of my master, yet here I have run into this vicious monster. Let me go and toy with him. If I succeed, I can seize the fiend and then rescue my master; it will not be too late.”

He lowered his cloud and looked carefully: there was the demon, sitting alone above and brazenly drinking wine and eating human flesh.
The Little Dragon laughed. “This wretch is no great shakes. He has betrayed himself and exposed his trail; now I know which way the wind blows, he is as good as a weight dropped into a broken basket.

p.src: What a fine Dragon King! With a shake of his body he transformed himself into a palace maid, truly light and graceful in figure and lovely in appearance. He hurried inside, curtsied to the demon, and said, “Prince Consort, please spare my life. I have come to pour your wine.” “Pour,” said the demon. The Little Dragon took the pot and poured wine into his cup until it rose several tenths of an inch above the rim without spilling. This was the Little Dragon’s “water-compelling art.” The monster did not recognize the trick and thought with delight, “So you possess such skill?” The Little Dragon said, “I can pour it higher still.” “Higher, then! Pour it higher!” said the monster. He raised the pot and kept pouring; the wine kept rising until it stood pointed and full like a thirteen-story jeweled pagoda, yet not a drop overflowed. The monster thrust out his mouth and drank a cupful; then he pulled the corpse toward him and took a bite. “Can you sing?” he asked. The Little Dragon replied, “I know a little.” He sang a little song in proper tune and rhythm, then served another cup. The monster asked, “Can you dance?” The Little Dragon said, “I know a little of that too, but with empty hands my dance will not be worth watching.” The monster lifted his robe, unfastened the jeweled sword at his waist, drew it from its sheath, and handed it to the Little Dragon.

p.src: The Little Dragon accepted the blade and, keeping his purpose firmly in mind, began dancing before the banquet table—three strokes upward, four downward, five to the left and six to the right—unfolding an elaborate display of sword flourishes. The monster stared until his eyes bulged. At the end of a flourish, the Little Dragon slashed at the fiend. The monster was no weakling: he twisted aside, and in his fluster snatched up a great red candelabrum to parry the jeweled blade. That great red candelabrum was forged from wrought iron and, including its handle, weighed eighty or ninety catties. The two burst out of the Silver Peace Hall. The Little Dragon resumed his true form, mounted a cloud, and fought the demon in midair. What a fierce battle they fought in the darkness! How did it appear?

p.src: The two fought for eight or nine rounds amid the clouds. The Little Dragon’s arms grew weak and his sinews numb, while the old demon remained strong and powerful. Unable to hold out, the Little Dragon sent the blade flying to cut down the monster. The monster knew how to catch a flying blade. With one hand he caught the jeweled sword, while with the other he swung down the great red candelabrum to strike. Caught unprepared, the Little Dragon took a blow on his hind leg. In panic he brought his cloud down. By good fortune the Imperial Water River saved his life, for he plunged headfirst beneath its waters. The demon pursued him but could not find him. Carrying the jeweled sword and the great red candelabrum, he returned to the Silver Peace Hall and, as before, drank himself to sleep. Of this we shall say no more.

p.src: For now we shall speak neither of Tripitaka’s calamity nor of the Little Dragon’s defeat. We turn instead to Zhu Bajie. After parting from Sha Wujing, he buried himself in a patch of grass and rooted out a hollow like a pig’s wallow. He slept straight through until midnight before waking. When he awoke, he had no idea where he was. He rubbed his eyes, collected his thoughts, and cocked an ear to listen. Ah! Deep in the mountains no dog barked; across the wilderness scarcely a cock crowed. Seeing the stars shift and the Dipper turn, he reckoned it was about the third watch and thought, “If I go back to rescue Sha Wujing, truly ‘a single strand makes no thread, and one hand cannot clap.’ Enough, enough! I will go into the city and see Master, report to His Majesty, and have him choose some more valiant troops to help old Zhu rescue Sha Wujing tomorrow.”

p.src: The fool hastily mounted a cloud and flew straight back to the city. In less than half a moment, he reached the posthouse. All was still, and the moon shone brightly. He searched both galleries but could not find his master. He saw only the white horse asleep over to one side, drenched all over, with a dark bruise the size of a plate on its hind leg. Bajie exclaimed in alarm, “Double misfortune! This poor devil has not been on the road, so why is his body covered in sweat and his leg bruised? Some villain must have robbed Master and beaten the horse lame.” The white horse recognized Bajie and suddenly spoke in a human voice, calling, “Elder Brother.” The fool was so frightened that he fell over. Scrambling up, he made to run outside. The white horse stretched forward, caught his black robe in its teeth, and said, “Brother, do not be afraid of me.” Trembling, Bajie said, “Brother, how is it that you have begun speaking today? If you are speaking at all, some great misfortune must surely have occurred.” The Little Dragon said, “Do you know that Master is in peril?” “I do not,” said Bajie. The Little Dragon said, “No, you do not. You and Sha Wujing displayed your prowess before the emperor, intending to bring down the demon and claim merit and reward. But unexpectedly the demon’s powers were great, while your skills proved insufficient, and you could not withstand him. Surely one of you should have returned to bring news, yet not a word was heard from either of you. The fiend transformed himself into a handsome scholar, entered the court, and claimed kinship with the emperor. He transformed our master into a magnificently striped tiger. I saw the ministers seize him and lock him in an iron cage in the court offices. When I heard of such suffering, my heart felt cut by a knife. You two had been absent for days and knew nothing of it. Fearing that Master might suddenly lose his life, I had no choice but to assume my dragon form and go to his rescue. But when I reached the court, I could not find him. When I reached the outside of the Silver Peace Hall, I encountered the fiend. I transformed myself again, this time into a palace maid, to deceive the monster. The monster told me to perform a sword dance for him, so I watched for an opening and slashed at him. But he dodged it at once, raised a great red candelabrum in both hands, and defeated me. I sent the blade flying at him, but he caught it, then swung down the great red candelabrum and struck me on the hind leg. That was why I plunged into the Imperial Water River and escaped with my life. The bruise on my leg was caused by his great red candelabrum.”

p.src: Hearing this, Bajie said, “Did all that truly happen?” The Little Dragon replied, “Would I lie to you?” Bajie said, “What are we to do? What are we to do? Can you still struggle to your feet?” The Little Dragon said, “And what if I can?” Bajie said, “If you can move, then struggle down to the sea. Old Zhu will shoulder the luggage and go back to Gao Family Village to become a son-in-law all over again.” At these words, the Little Dragon caught Bajie’s robe in his teeth and refused to let go. Tears streamed uncontrollably from his eyes as he said, “Elder Brother, whatever you do, you must not give in to idleness.” Bajie said, “And what else can I do? Brother Sha has already been captured, and I cannot defeat that monster. If we do not break up now, what are we waiting for?”

p.src: The young dragon pondered for a long while, then shed tears and said, “Brother, do not speak of giving up. If you wish to save Master, you need only go and fetch one person.” Bajie asked, “Whom would you have me fetch?” The young dragon replied, “Make haste and ride the clouds back to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, and invite our eldest brother, Sun the Pilgrim, to come. He still possesses mighty powers for subduing demons. He is certain to save Master and avenge our defeat as well.” Bajie said, “Brother, let us ask someone else instead. That monkey and I do not get along. Earlier, on White Tiger Ridge, he killed the White-Bone Lady, and he blamed me for urging Master to recite the Band-Tightening Spell. I meant it only as a joke, but I never imagined that old monk would truly begin reciting it and then drive him away. Who knows how bitterly he resents me? He certainly will not come. And if some word of mine happens to offend him, that mourning staff of his is heavy. If he forgets his strength and gives me a few blows, how could I possibly survive?” The young dragon said, “He will certainly not strike you. He is a Monkey King of benevolence and honor. When you see him, say nothing of Master’s peril. Say only, ‘Master misses you.’ Coax him into coming. Once here, when he sees what has happened, he is bound to be enraged and will surely fight that fiend. He will certainly capture it and save our master.” Bajie said, “Very well, very well. You are so devoted that if I refused to go, it would make me seem lacking in devotion. I shall go. If the Pilgrim truly agrees to come, I will return with him; but if he refuses, do not wait for me, for I shall not return either.” The young dragon said, “Go, go. I guarantee that he will come.”

p.src: So the fool gathered up his rake, straightened his robe, leapt into the air, mounted a cloud, and headed directly east. This time, too, the Tang Monk was fated to survive. The fool happened to catch a following wind. He spread his two ears like sails, swiftly crossed the Eastern Ocean, and brought his cloud down. Before he knew it, the sun had risen, and he entered the mountain to search for a path.

p.src: As he went along, he suddenly heard voices. When Bajie looked carefully, he saw the Pilgrim in a mountain hollow, surrounded by a host of lesser demons. He sat atop a rocky cliff, with more than twelve hundred monkeys before him, arrayed in ranks and files, crying, “Long life to our lord and grandsire, the Great Sage!” Bajie thought, “What splendid comfort! What splendid comfort! No wonder he refused to remain a monk and insisted on coming home. So this is the good life he enjoys—a vast estate and all these young monkeys to wait upon him. If old Pig had a mountain domain like this, I would not be any sort of monk either. But now that I have come here, what am I to do? I must see him, one way or another.” The fool was somewhat afraid of him and dared not present himself openly. Instead, he slunk along the grassy cliff until he had squeezed among the twelve or thirteen hundred monkeys, where he kowtowed along with them.

p.src: But the Great Sage sat high above, and his eyes were exceedingly sharp. He saw Bajie clearly and asked, “Who is that stranger bowing out of order among the ranks? Where has he come from? Bring him up here.” Before he had finished speaking, the young monkeys swarmed around Bajie, shoved him forward, and pinned him to the ground. The Pilgrim asked, “Where have you come from, stranger?” With his head lowered, Bajie said, “I hardly dare accept the honor of your question. I am no stranger, but an old acquaintance—an old acquaintance.” The Pilgrim said, “All the monkeys under this Great Sage’s command look much alike. But your face is made quite differently, and your appearance is rather lumpy. You must be a demon from elsewhere. If you have come from elsewhere wishing to join my command, you should first have submitted your credentials and reported your name, so that I might enroll you in the ranks and assign you a post. If I have not accepted you, how dare you bow here in such disorder?” Bajie kept his head down, thrust out his snout, and said, “Shameless though it is, here is this face of mine for you to see. You and I were brothers for several years, yet you pretend not to know me and call me some stranger.” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “Raise your head and let me look at you.” The fool tilted his snout upward and said, “Look, then. Even if you do not recognize me, surely you recognize this snout.” Unable to contain his laughter, the Pilgrim said, “Zhu Bajie!” The moment he heard himself named, Bajie rolled over, sprang to his feet, and cried, “That is right, that is right! I am Zhu Bajie.” Then he thought, “Now that he recognizes me, it will be easy to talk.”

p.src: The Pilgrim said, “Why are you here instead of accompanying the Tang Monk to fetch the scriptures? I suppose you offended Master and he banished you home as well. Show me whatever writ of banishment he gave you.” Bajie said, “I did not offend him. He gave me no writ of banishment, nor did he drive me away.” The Pilgrim asked, “If you have no writ and were not driven away, why have you come here?” Bajie replied, “Master misses you and sent me to invite you back.” The Pilgrim said, “He neither invites me nor misses me. That day he swore before Heaven and wrote the writ of banishment in his own hand. Why would he now miss me and send you all this way to fetch me? I most certainly ought not to go.” Bajie invented a lie on the spot and hurriedly said, “He truly does miss you—he truly does!” The Pilgrim asked, “How did he come to miss me?” Bajie said, “Master was riding along when he called, ‘Disciple!’ I failed to hear him, and Friar Sand pretended to be deaf. That made Master think of you. He said we were useless, while you were clever and quick-witted, always answering the instant he called and giving ten answers to a single question. Because he missed you in that way, he expressly sent me to invite you. I earnestly beg you to come. First, you will not disappoint his longing; second, you will not let my long journey go for nothing.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim leapt down from the cliff, took Bajie by the arm, and said, “Good brother, you have had a tiring journey. Come and amuse yourself with me for a while.” Bajie said, “Brother, this place is far away. I fear Master will grow anxious if we return late, so I shall not stay to play.” The Pilgrim said, “Since you have come all this way, why not see what you think of my mountain scenery?” The fool dared not refuse too insistently, so he had no choice but to stroll along with him.

p.src: The two of them talked and laughed for a long while, then descended the mountain. Beside the road they saw several little monkeys kneeling there, holding bunches of richly purple grapes, fragrant pears and dates, golden loquats, and bright-red waxberries. They called out, “Great Sage, venerable grandfather, please take some breakfast.” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “My brother Pig has a mighty appetite; fruit is hardly a meal for him. Still, never mind, never mind. Do not think the offering too meager; make do with a few as a snack.” Bajie said, “Though I have a mighty appetite, I can still follow the customs of the place I am in. Bring them here, bring them here. I too shall eat a few and taste the fresh fruit.”

p.src: After the two had eaten the fruit, the sun gradually rose higher. Fearing that they might be too late to rescue the Tang Monk, the fool kept urging him, “Brother, Master is waiting there in hope of our return. Please come away with me at once.” The Pilgrim said, “Worthy brother, why not go into the Water Curtain Cave and amuse yourself for a while?” Bajie firmly declined, saying, “I am most grateful for your kind invitation, brother, but Master has been waiting a long time. I shall not trouble you by entering the cave.” The Pilgrim said, “Since that is so, I shall not presume to detain you. Let us bid farewell here.” Bajie said, “Brother, are you not coming?” The Pilgrim said, “Where would I go? Here neither Heaven calls me to account nor Earth governs me; I am free and easy. If I cannot enjoy myself, why should I be a monk at all? I am not going. Go by yourself. Just tell the Tang Monk this from me: since he drove me away, he must never think of me again.” Hearing this, the fool dared not press him too hard, fearing that he might provoke his temper and receive a couple of blows from the cudgel. With no other choice, he meekly took his leave, found the road, and departed.

p.src: When the Pilgrim saw him leave, he immediately ordered two nimble little monkeys to follow Bajie and listen to what he said. Sure enough, after the fool had descended the mountain and gone no more than three or four li, he turned back, pointed toward the Pilgrim, and cursed aloud, “That monkey! Instead of being a monk, he has turned himself into a monster. That macaque! I came with the best intentions to invite him back, yet he refuses to go. Well, if you will not go, so be it.” He would walk a few steps, then curse a few more times. The two little monkeys hurried back and reported, “Great Sage, venerable grandfather, that Zhu Bajie is not behaving honestly. Every so often as he walks, he curses you.” The Pilgrim flew into a rage and cried, “Bring him back here!” The whole troop of monkeys came flying over the ground and caught up with Bajie. They knocked him headlong, seized his bristles, tugged his ears, pulled his tail, and yanked his hair, then captured him and carried him back.
